title: Seat Newcomers Far Apart
statement:
A waiting room has n chairs in one row, numbered 0 to n − 1. People arrive and leave one at a time. Each newcomer picks the free chair that is farthest from the nearest occupied chair. If several chairs tie, they take the lowest-numbered one. In an empty room they take chair 0.

  • SpacedSeating(n) creates an empty room with n chairs.
  • sit() seats a newcomer by the rule above and returns their chair number. It is only called when at least one chair is free.
  • leave(chair) frees that chair. It is only called on an occupied chair.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the object. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor and for leave).

examples.why: Chair 9 is 9 away from chair 0. Then 4 sits mid-way (distance 4). Chairs 2 and 6 both give distance 2, so the lower one wins. After 4 leaves, the gap from 2 to 9 is widest, and chair 5 is 3 away from both sides.
Once chair 0 is free, sitting at the very end puts you 3 away from chair 3, which beats the middle of the gap 3–7 (only 2). Ends only have a neighbour on one side.

constraints: At most 100 000 calls to sit and leave in total
hints: Only the occupied chairs matter. Between two neighbouring occupied chairs a and b, where is the best chair, and how far is it from the nearest person?

Inside a gap the best chair is the midpoint, at distance (b − a) / 2 rounded down. The two ends are special: chair 0 is first away from the first person, and chair n − 1 is n − 1 − last away from the last. Scanning a sorted list of occupied chairs gives O(k) per call.

Keep every gap in a max-heap ordered by (distance, then lower chair). A leave merges two gaps into one; instead of deleting the old ones from the heap, mark them stale and skip them when they reach the top.

explain.intuition:
The room is described by its occupied chairs, and the choices live in the gaps between them. In a gap between occupied chairs a and b, the best spot is the middle, a + ⌊(b − a) / 2⌋, at distance ⌊(b − a) / 2⌋. The edges of the row are half-gaps: the left edge offers chair 0 at distance first, the right edge chair n − 1 at distance n − 1 − last. That is why an end chair often beats a middle seat.

A sorted list of occupied chairs lets you scan all gaps per call, which is O(k). To do better, keep the gaps in a heap keyed by (distance, chair). sit pops the best gap and splits it in two; leave joins the two gaps around the chair into one. Old gaps stay in the heap, but a next map from each chair to its right neighbour tells you whether a popped gap (a, b) still exists: it does only if next[a] == b.
steps: Use sentinels −1 and n as virtual walls. Keep maps next and prev between neighbouring occupied chairs, starting with next[−1] = n, and push the gap (−1, n).
For a gap (a, b): if a = −1 the chair is 0 at distance b; if b = n the chair is n − 1 at distance n − 1 − a; otherwise the midpoint. Skip gaps with no free chair.
sit(): pop until the top gap is current (next[a] == b). Seat its chair s, link a → s → b, push gaps (a, s) and (s, b), return s.
leave(p): look up a = prev[p], b = next[p], link a → b, forget p, push gap (a, b).
pitfalls: Treating the ends like middle gaps. Chair 0 with the first person at 3 is 3 away, not 1.
Breaking ties toward the higher chair, or comparing only distances in the heap. The lower chair must win a tie.
Forgetting that n can be 10⁹. Any approach that loops over chairs instead of occupied chairs is far too slow.

complexity.time: O(log k) amortized per call with the heap (O(k) with a sorted list)

solutions.title: Sorted list of occupied chairs
solutions.idea: Scan the left edge, every gap and the right edge, keep the best chair with a strict comparison so ties go to the lower chair, then insert it in sorted position.

solutions.title: Heap of gaps with lazy deletion
solutions.idea: Every gap between neighbours sits in a max-heap keyed by (distance, lower chair). A neighbour map tells whether a popped gap is still current.

followups: Without lazy deletion, which ordered structure lets you remove the two old gaps directly on leave?
Chairs are now arranged in a circle, so chair n − 1 is next to chair 0. What changes?
